title: How to reduce your risk of injury from exercise or physical activity | NHS inform
text:
How to reduce your risk of injury from exercise or physical activity
Exercise and physical activity are important for both your physical and mental health.
The information on this page provides tips and considerations when doing exercise.
Warm up for exercise
Warming up prepares you to exercise. This includes:
increasing your heart rate in preparation for exercise
dynamic stretching
strength and balance exercises
sport or activity specific movement
A warm-up should take around 10 to 15 minutes.
Increasing your heart rate
Gradually increasing your heart rate and body temperature helps get your joints, muscles and tendons ready for activity.
Depending on the activity you are about to do, you could walk briskly whilst swinging your arms then gently jog or cycle.
Dynamic stretching
Dynamic stretching involves controlled, movement-based exercises to prepare your body for activity. This should be done after you’ve warmed up. This is done by moving muscles and joints through their full range of motion.
Some examples of dynamic stretching are:
forward and backward lunges
high knees
hip circles
forward and backward leg swings
shoulder rotations
trunk rotations
Strength and balance training
Strength training increases your muscle and tendon resilience. Balance improves your reactions, your body awareness and your co-ordination.
Some examples of combined strength and balance training are:
single-leg squats ensuring the knee moves forward over the middle of your foot
single-leg heel raises
single-leg balancing
wall slides
shoulder rotation with weights or resistance bands
It’s important to include these types of exercises in your weekly activity. They can also be used as part of a warm-up.
Sport or activity specific movement
Depending on your activity, you may also have specific warming up exercises or drills. These could be:
ball-passing in ball sports
back, neck and hip rotations in golf
light contact in rugby
light swings in racquet sports
walking drills for running
Examples of sport specific warm-ups include
FIFA 11+
for football,
Activate
in rugby or the
The KNEE Programme
for netball. These can be used for other sports.
Recovery after exercise or physical activity
It’s important to allow your body to recover from your activity. It takes over 24 hours to recover from an intense session of exercise.
There are many things you can do to aid your recovery.
Cool-down after activity
Cooling down should happen straight after your activity. It helps to reduce your heart rate slowly. This also helps your body remove lactic acid from your muscles which builds up during exercise.
You can reduce your heart rate by going from running to a slow jog and then a slow jog to a walk. A cool down should take around 5-10 minutes.
Hydration and nutrition
Following exercise ensure you drink fluids. Try to drink something that helps replace the electrolytes in your body.
Having a light snack after exercising containing carbohydrate and protein is also recommended. Protein helps muscles repair and carbohydrate helps restore energy.
Sleep
Sleep is important after exercise to help the body recover. It’s also important to ensure you have slept well before activity. This ensures the body is prepared for exercise and improves performance.
Read more about how to improve your sleep
Managing load and training errors
Many injuries occur due to repetitive overloading of tissues particularly bones and tendons. As well as ensuring these are strong it’s important to avoid overloading these tissues and develop overuse injuries.
Starting to run for the first time
NHS England has a
Couch to 5k programme
that can help you start running. If you’re not active your first steps should be build up a walking program.
Once you can walk for 30-40 minutes you’re ready to start a running program.
Once you’re up and running
You should always follow a recognised training plan. Many organised running events provide suggested training plans.
When building up running, stick to the 10% rule. Only progress the amount you run by 10% or less a week. Wearables like smart watches and phones can help monitor your running.
Rest and recovery days
It’s important to build in days where you allow your body to rest and recover.
You should:
avoid consecutive days training in the same sport
ensure at least one rest day per week from training
have a recovery day where you do light activity and movement like swimming or gentle walking
Resistance training
If muscles and tendons are strong, they’ll have increased capacity to handle the demands of exercise.
Resistance training can include strength training in the gym.
You should aim to do 2 resistance training sessions a week.
Read about the recommended physical activity guidelines
Footwear and equipment
Footwear should be specific to the sport, supportive and comfortable. You should try to renew your footwear when you start to see signs of excessive wear.
Sport specific equipment
Some sports have specific safety equipment.
Mouthguards or gumshields can protect against facial and mouth injuries. Ensure they are well-fitting.
Head gear in ice hockey and lacrosse can protect against concussion.
Shin guards in football and hockey can protect against impact injuries.
Rules
Rules are there to protect you. Following the rules of sport can reduce likelihood of injury. The tackle height rule in rugby or the body checking rule in ice hockey can reduce concussion and spinal injuries.
Read about the if in doubt sit them out guidelines for concussion management
Nutrition
Having a balanced diet while you exercise can help the body recover but also refuel it for the next bout of activity.
Ensure you are taking enough calories for your activity level.
Read about how to eat a healthy balanced diet
Not taking in enough calories can lead to:
fatigue
underperformance
metabolic problems
lower bone density
All of these can increase the likelihood of an injury.
How to manage injuries
Read more about injuries to specific parts of the body:
neck problems
back problems
chest and rib injury
arm, shoulder and hand problems
leg and foot problems
